---
title: "Laboratories"
description: "Slider-driven figures for a kernel density estimate, a Beta–Binomial update, a finite Markov chain, and the coverage of a confidence interval."
---

A laboratory on this site is a figure with the population known, so the error is visible. The controls change one piece of a model. Where a formula exists, the figure uses it. A simulation or a normal approximation is labelled as one.

The kernel density page came first. The other three are the same idea for a prior, a transition matrix, and a confidence interval.

## Kernel density

A Gaussian kernel turns a sample into a density.<sup id="cite_ref-1" class="cite-ref" data-cite-key="rosenblatt1956"><a href="#cite_note-1" title="Rosenblatt (1956) — Remarks on Some Nonparametric Estimates of a Density Function">[1]</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-2" class="cite-ref" data-cite-key="parzen1962"><a href="#cite_note-2" title="Parzen (1962) — On Estimation of a Probability Density Function and Mode">[2]</a></sup> The bandwidth $h$ is the choice.<sup id="cite_ref-3" class="cite-ref" data-cite-key="silverman1986"><a href="#cite_note-3" title="Silverman (1986) — Density Estimation for Statistics and Data Analysis">[3]</a></sup> A small $h$ leaves a bump on the observations: high variance, low bias. A large $h$ washes the modes out. The page keeps the sample still and moves $h$, and it plots that sample's integrated squared error against the mean integrated squared error of a sample of the same size. The estimate does not use the true density. Both errors do.

[Open the kernel density laboratory](kernel-density.qmd).

## Beta–Binomial updating

A coin has unknown heads probability $\theta$, and the prior is a Beta distribution. After $x$ heads in $n$ tosses the posterior is $\mathrm{Beta}(\alpha+x,\beta+n-x)$.<sup id="cite_ref-4" class="cite-ref" data-cite-key="bayes1763"><a href="#cite_note-4" title="Bayes (1763) — An essay towards solving a problem in the doctrine of chances. By the late Rev. Mr. Bayes, F. R. S. communicated by Mr. Price, in a letter to John Canton, A. M. F. R. S">[4]</a></sup> The posterior mean is a weighted average of the prior mean and $x/n$, with weight $(\alpha+\beta)/(\alpha+\beta+n)$ on the prior. Future tosses are predicted by the beta–binomial average over that posterior, which is wider than a binomial that fixes $\theta$ at the posterior mean.

[Open the Beta–Binomial laboratory](beta-binomial.qmd).

## A Markov chain

On a finite set of states the whole process is a transition matrix $P$.<sup id="cite_ref-5" class="cite-ref" data-cite-key="markov1906"><a href="#cite_note-5" title="Markov (1906) — Rasprostranenie zakona bol&#x27;shikh chisel na velichiny, zavisyashchie drug ot druga [Extension of the law of large numbers to quantities depending on each other]">[5]</a></sup> From a chosen start, the distribution after $t$ steps is the corresponding row of $P^{t}$. A stationary distribution satisfies $\pi=\pi P$. When the chain is one closed aperiodic class, every start forgets itself and $P^{t}$ settles on $\pi$. A periodic chain can have a stationary distribution while $P^{t}$ keeps oscillating. Two closed classes mean two stationary distributions, and one path's time average follows the class the path happens to enter.

[Open the Markov chain laboratory](markov-chain.qmd).

## Coverage of a confidence interval

The confidence is the probability, before the sample is drawn, that the random interval contains the parameter. This page draws the interval repeatedly from a known population and marks the misses. For a normal sample the $t$ interval hits with probability exactly equal to the stated level.<sup id="cite_ref-6" class="cite-ref" data-cite-key="student1908"><a href="#cite_note-6" title="Student (1908) — The Probable Error of a Mean">[6]</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-7" class="cite-ref" data-cite-key="neyman1937"><a href="#cite_note-7" title="Neyman (1937) — Outline of a Theory of Statistical Estimation Based on the Classical Theory of Probability">[7]</a></sup> Using a normal quantile with the sample standard deviation $s$ hits less often. For a proportion, the exact coverage of the Wald and Wilson intervals is a sum over the binomial distribution, and Wald's sum falls away from the stated level when the probability is near $0$ or $1$.<sup id="cite_ref-8" class="cite-ref" data-cite-key="wilson1927"><a href="#cite_note-8" title="Wilson (1927) — Probable Inference, the Law of Succession, and Statistical Inference">[8]</a></sup>

[Open the confidence interval laboratory](ci-coverage.qmd).
